title: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography XI — a Roman merchant and a Persian argue before the king of Sri Lanka, and the king decides it by weighing their two coins
language_note:
THIS RECORD CARRIES NO SOURCE-LANGUAGE TEXT AND THE `language_code` SAYS SO. The tier is `published_translation_only` and the only text on the record is McCrindle's English. The Greek of the Christian Topography is not transcribed here, was not captured, and is not claimed.

AND `original_text_excerpt` IS OMITTED RATHER THAN FILLED WITH A PLACEHOLDER, raising the loader warning `empty original_text_excerpt, no original chunk emitted`. That is `africa-07-cosmas-sasu`'s treatment of the same author in the same edition, and FINDING 80 is what the alternative costs.
date: Written c. 550 CE. Cosmas dates the episode himself, in the passage: Sopatrus `has now been dead these five and thirty years past`, so the audience before the king falls a generation or more before the writing. McCrindle's edition is dated 1897 and this passage sits at his pages 368–370, in Book XI.
reference_translation: [338] Now I must here relate what happened to one of our countrymen, a merchant called Sopatrus, who used to go thither on business, but who to our knowledge has now been dead these five and thirty years past. Once on a time he came to this island of Taprobane on business, and as it chanced a vessel from Persia put into port at the same time with himself. So the men from Adulé with whom Sopatrus was, went ashore, as did likewise the people of Persia, with whom came a person of venerable age and appearance.46 Then, as the way there was, the chief men of the place and the custom-house officers received them and brought them to the king. The king having admitted them to an audience and received their salutations, requested them to be seated. Then he asked them: In what state are your countries, and how go things with them? To this they replied, they go well. Afterwards, as the conversation proceeded, the king inquired Which of your kings is the greater and the more powerful? The elderly Persian snatching the word answered: Our king is both the more powerful and the greater and richer, and indeed is King of Kings, and whatsoever he |369 desires, that he is able to do. Sopatrus on the other hand sat mute. So the king asked: Have you, Roman,47 nothing to say? What have I to say, he rejoined, when he there has said such things? but if you wish to learn the truth you have the two kings here present. Examine each and you will see which of them is the grander and the more powerful. The king on hearing this was amazed at his words and asked, How say you that I have both the kings here? You have, replied Sopatrus, the money 48 of both ---- the nomisma 49 of the one, and the drachma, that is, the miliarision 50 of the other. Examine the image of each, and you will see the truth. The king thought well of the suggestion, and, nodding his consent, ordered both the coins to be produced. Now the Roman coin had a right good ring, was of bright metal and finely shaped, for pieces of this kind are picked for export to the island. But the miliarision, to say it in one word, was of silver, and not to be compared with the gold coin. So the king after he had turned them this way and that, and had attentively examined both, highly commended the nomisma, saying that the Romans were certainly a splendid, powerful, and |370 sagacious people.51 So he ordered great honour to be paid to Sopatrus, causing him to be mounted on an elephant, and conducted round the city with drums beating and high state. These circumstances were told us by Sopatrus himself and his companions, who had accompanied him to that island from Adule; and as they told the story, the Persian was deeply chagrined at what had occurred.

EVERY MARK IN IT IS THE EDITION'S OR THE TRANSCRIBER'S AND NONE IS REPAIRED. `46`, `47`, `48`, `49`, `50` and `51` are McCrindle's footnote numbers, left where they fall against `appearance.46`, `Roman,47`, `the money 48` and `sagacious people.51`; `|369` and `|370` are his page boundaries; `[338]` is the transcription's own marker; and `----` is how the 2003 transcription renders a long dash. THE EDITION IS ALSO INCONSISTENT WITH ITSELF AND THAT IS KEPT: the port is spelled `Adulé` at the start of the passage and `Adule` at the end, twenty lines apart, and both stand.

WHERE THE PASSAGE IS CUT, AND WHY THERE. It begins where Cosmas announces the story and ends on the Persian's chagrin, which is the last clause of the episode; the next sentence turns to the White Huns and Gollas and his two thousand elephants. Nothing is elided inside it.

THE BOUNDARY OF THE TRANSLATION SEARCH, AND THIS RECORD OWES IT AS MUCH AS ANY OTHER IN THE TIER. What was looked at: this transcription of McCrindle 1897, which is the standard English and is out of copyright. What was NOT opened: **Wanda Wolska-Conus's `Topographie chrétienne` (Sources chrétiennes 141, 159, 197, 1968–73)**, the modern critical edition with a French translation, which would give the Greek this record does not carry and a reading later than 1897 — it is in copyright and nothing reachable from this project establishes what it says; and **the manuscripts**, Vaticanus gr. 699 and the Sinai and Florence copies. No claim is made about any of them. THE SEARCH STOPPED AT THE PUBLIC-DOMAIN ENGLISH, which is exactly what a `published_translation_only` record is.

THE SAME BOUNDARY `africa-07-cosmas-sasu` STATED IN F6, AND IT IS RESTATED RATHER THAN CROSS-REFERENCED. A boundary a record points at instead of stating is a boundary a later reader has to go and find; and the two records could in principle have searched differently, so each says what it did.

ONE THING THE TRANSCRIPTION CARRIES THAT THIS RECORD DOES NOT TAKE. McCrindle's footnote 47 quotes Tennent's `Ceylon` on the king addressing Sopatrus as `Rwmeu~` — the Greek word behind `Roman` — and footnote 46 records that Montfaucon read the Persian's `presbu&thj` as an ambassador rather than an old man. **Both are on the same page, both bear directly on this passage, and neither is in the excerpt**, because they are the editor's apparatus and not the translation. They are named here so that a later block knows the apparatus exists and where it is.

notes:
F7's South Asia `published_translation_only` slot. Seventh and last record of the tranche, fifty-fourth in the corpus, AND IT CLOSES THE TIER AT 4 OF 4.

WHAT THE PASSAGE IS. A Roman merchant from Adulé and a Persian ship put into Taprobane on the same day. Both parties are brought before the king, who asks which of their kings is the greater. The Persian answers first and at length — King of Kings, richer, more powerful, able to do whatever he desires. Sopatrus says nothing, and then says: you have both kings here, look at their money. The king has the two coins brought out, turns them over, and gives the verdict to the gold. Sopatrus is put on an elephant and paraded round the city with drums.

**THIS IS THE ONLY RECORD IN THE CORPUS WHERE ROME AND PERSIA ARE JUDGED AGAINST EACH OTHER BY SOMEBODY WHO IS NEITHER.** Everything else the corpus holds about that rivalry is one of the two parties speaking: `persia-01-skz` is Shapur listing the emperors he defeated; `persia-05-abnun` is a Sasanian inscription; the Chinese accounts describe Fu-lin bordering Po-si without adjudicating between them. Here a South Asian king is the judge, the courtroom is his, and the evidence is two coins.

AND THE CRITERION IS METALLURGY, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES IT WORTH HAVING. The king does not weigh armies or territory. He weighs the ring, the brightness and the shaping of a gold nomisma against a silver miliarision — and Cosmas, who is not a disinterested witness, adds the detail that undercuts his own story if you read it carefully: `pieces of this kind are picked for export to the island`. The coins that reach Sri Lanka are selected. `southasia-07-bm-claudius-aureus`, curated in this same tranche, is one of those exported pieces at the other end of its life, with a chisel through the emperor's head.

WHAT THE TIER LOOKS LIKE NOW THAT IT IS CLOSED. Four records: `africa-01-ezana-stone`, a placeholder whose translation is a titulature from a news website; `africa-07-cosmas-sasu`, McCrindle on the Aksumite gold expedition; `eastasia-09-jiutangshu-fulin`, Hirth on the Tang court's account of Byzantium; and this. **THREE OF THE FOUR ARE A REGION SPOKEN ABOUT AND ONE IS A REGION SPEAKING**, and that was declared in `F7_CURATION_START.md` before either F7 record existed rather than discovered here. `published_translation_only` does not count toward the per-region source-language floor and FINDING 68's provenance line will not move, so nothing in the repository reports it. It is reported here.

THE SECOND COST DECLARED IN ADVANCE, ALSO IN THE CURATION START: this is the same author, the same translator, the same edition, the same transcriber and the same site as `africa-07-cosmas-sasu`, curated one day earlier. Two of the tier's four members come from one 1897 book. The alternative examined and refused was Varāhamihira's `Pañcasiddhāntikā` — a South Asian text whose second siddhānta is named for Rome — whose only reachable English is OCR of an 1889 scan with damage inside the translated verses. A digest proves the corpus copied a damaged text faithfully; it cannot repair it.

RULING 79's P2 IS NOT ABOUT THIS RECORD BUT ITS MECHANISM MIGHT BE. `africa-07-cosmas-sasu` — the same author, translator and genre — crowded the two Adulis trade pairs in F6's run and nothing else. This record names Adulé twice and Taprobane, Persia, India's pepper marts and the Roman nomisma. If the resemblance mechanism holds, its chunks should appear against Indian Ocean trade targets ACROSS regions rather than in South Asia alone.

NOT DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE, and it is the fifth F7 record of which that is true. F7 holds one declaration, Block F's last, spent on `persia-07-met-ewer-anahita`.

THE ID WAS FOUND THROUGH THE NAMES DUMP AND CONFIRMED ON DESCRIPTION AND COORDINATE BEFORE IT WAS TAKEN. `--find "Taprobane"` against the pinned 2026-08-10 places dump returns no title match and one unrelated mountain whose description mentions the island; the names dump returns three attested names on one id — `Taprobane`, `Ταπροβάνη` and `Insvla Taproba[n]e`, all 50298. Entry 50298 was then read out of the places dump directly: title `Sri Lanka`, description `The island of Sri Lanka lies at the center of the Indian Ocean world, connecting and connected by trade and communication with and between Africa, Arabia, southwest Asia, peninsular south Asia, Southeast Asia, Oceania, and beyond.`, reprLat 7.98139972411, reprLong 80.574678177, featureTypes `island`, locationPrecision `related`, -330..2100, periods including `roman` and `late-antique`. THIS IS THE SECOND TIME `--names-dump` HAS BEEN THE ONLY ROUTE TO AN ID — `pleiades:39379` for Maʾrib surfaced the same way, as the Greek `Μαρίαβα` — and it is why the flag exists. A name match is not an identification; this one was confirmed before it was used.

FIRST TIME THIS CORPUS PLACES ANYTHING IN SRI LANKA.

subject_places.name: Adulé — the Red Sea port Sopatrus and his companions sail from
subject_places.note:
`stated` because the excerpt names it twice — `the men from Adulé with whom Sopatrus was` and `who had accompanied him to that island from Adule`, with the edition spelling it two ways. THE ID IS THE ONE `africa-03-periplus-adulis` AND `africa-05-adulis-throne` ALREADY CARRY, and it was re-read from `data/gazetteer.json` in this session rather than inherited: `pleiades:39271`, title `Adouli`, description `An ancient market settlement and port on the west coast of the Red Sea near modern Zula in Eritrea.`

AND THIS IS THE FIRST TIME THE CORPUS DRAWS AN EDGE OUT OF ADULIS RATHER THAN INTO IT. `africa-03-periplus-adulis` is Roman goods arriving at the port; `africa-05-adulis-throne` is an inscription standing there; `africa-07-cosmas-sasu` is an expedition going inland from the kingdom behind it. This is a ship leaving Adulé for Sri Lanka, and the man on it is a Roman.

subject_places.name: The Roman world — whose nomisma is picked for export to the island
subject_places.note:
NO ID, AND EMPHATICALLY NOT PLEIADES 423025 `Roma`. The passage names no Roman city; it names `Roman`, `the Romans` and `our king`, which are a people, an adjective and an office. `southasia-07-bm-claudius-aureus` in this same tranche DOES take 423025, because its source names Rome the city as a mint — the contrast between the two entries is the rule working in both directions on one day.

`source` is textually grounded and not inferred: `pieces of this kind are picked for export to the island`. Roman gold moves to Taprobane, in the source's own clause, and the selection is the source's own admission.
